## General Overview

The structure of important files in the template is shown below.  Note there are other files in several of the other directories, but this outlines the files we want to pay careful attention to.

```
<your github username>.github.io/
├── _data/
│   ├── programming-skills.yml
│   ├── other-skills.yml
│   └── timeline.yml
├── _example_posts/
├── _example_projects/
├── includes/
├── layouts/
├── _plugins/
├── _posts/
├── _projects/
│   └── 1_Vega_lite_project.md
├── assets/
│   ├── jsons/
│   └── pngs/
├── pages/
│   ├── projects.html
│   └── about.md
├── python_notebooks/
├── README.md
├── Gemfile
└── _config.yml
```

### Summary of commands

Here is the list of commands to reference for updating your page locally and pushing those changes to your remote github.io page.

#### Installation (already completed in course)

This should already be accomplished in Lab \#6 but in brief:
1. Create and clone a [github.io pages instance](https://docs.github.com/en/pages)
2. [Install](https://jekyllrb.com/docs/installation/) Ruby (~version 3.4) and Jekyll
3. [Download the template](https://github.com/jnaiman/online_cv_public), move files into your github.io pages instance locally
4. Install gems with `bundle install` in your local github.io pages directory

#### Serving files locally

Use `bundle exec jekyll serve` in your github.io directory to host your webpage (note you will have to manually refresh your webpage each time you modify your local files).

For "live" reloading instead use `bundle exec jekyll serve -l`.  Note: you can only use live reloads for one locally hosted page at a time (otherwise you will get a long and nebulous error).

**If you change the `_config.yml` file you will have to kill (`CTRL+C`) and restart the serve command.** All other files will automatically update changes to your locally served webpage if you use the `-l` option.

#### Pushing changes to your remote github.io remote 

For this you will use the same commands you used in Lab \#6 in the Terminal/Anaconda Prompt (make sure you have git installed\!):
  * `git pull` (ONLY IF you have edited things online in your repo)  
  * `git status` (to see changes)  
  * `git add -A` (add all changes)  
  * `git commit -m` "message" (commit changes)  
  * `git push` (push all changes)

**Files and Folders**

Before modifying anything major in our template, let’s take a tour\!  In our template directory we see the following:

![][image1]  
Each of these files/directories is a part of constructing our fully interactive webpage, so let’s look at them one at a time.

**README.md**

This file is where you can give anybody that stumbles across the repository a bit more info about the source code.  In a text editor, it will look something like:

![][image2]

Which, if you go to the [online\_cv GitHub repository](https://github.com/jnaiman/online_cv_public) gets rendered to:  
![][image3]

You will not generally have to modify anything in this file.

**Gemfile**

This file tells bundler what to install that is needed for our project.  In this case, some jekyll stuff and some github pages stuff.  
![][image4]  
When you run “bundle install” bundler takes this file and creates a “Gemfile.lock” with all of the specific versions of packages that are installed (we won’t be looking at that but you can check yours out if you want).

You don’t need to generally modify this file, but if you create your own webpage not using the template, you might have to install other packages.

**\_config.yml** 

This file is the first file we’ll really start modifying.  In this file you’ll see a lot of ways to modify the different parameters in your webpage.

![][image5]

At the top you see some instructions of how to modify this page.  What we will do is fill in your new info, re-build the webpage with “bundle exec jekyll serve” to see our new webpage and then push these changes to our github.io pages repository when we are happy with those changes.

Let’s try this by changing one thing first, the title – right now its PossibleCorg, but you probably want something different\!

![][image6]

We’ll walk through this, **but don’t do it yet** (we still need to update things for your page\!) 

* Change this to “\<Last Name\> Resume”  
* Run “bundle exec jekyll serve” and see what happens locally  
* Push to github, in the Terminal/Anaconda Prompt (make sure you have git installed\!) do:  
  * git pull (ONLY IF you have edited things online in your repo)  
  * git status (to see changes)  
  * git add \-A (add all changes)  
  * git commit \-m “message” (commit changes)  
  * git push (push all changes)  
  * NOTE\!\!: if you have edited things online you will get a merge warning, you need to download your repository (“git pull”) and merge (“git merge”) and then commit this (“git commit \-m”) – it will be easier if you do everything locally instead of using the GUI\!  
* After some build time, your new Environment with your changes will be updated on your github.io page under the /online\_cv\_public sub-heading

So, this process takes a bit of a while to build to a full, hosted webpage, so generally, we’ll just host locally and check out some changes when we re-build and then we’ll push to our github.io repository when we have done enough changes.  Also\! We haven’t updated things to point to your specific github page\!  So this won’t work. Let’s work on that.

A few other items in this file that might be interesting to change:  
![][image7]  
Update the description to say a little bit about yourself.

![][image8]  
Make sure this points to \*your\* GitHub page\!  This should be your user name (see the description).

Another thing you probably want to change in the future, is the link – if you want this as your main github.io page (i.e. where employers will “land” if they come to your github.io page) you can set the “baseurl” to just empty quotes “”:  
![][image9]  
Since we are still working on things, we’ll leave it as is and see that we need to add this part to the URL when we want to see our build on our github.io page.

Some other things we might want to change are our name, the image that we use for ourselves, and then any relevant links we want to appear as icons under our name:  
![][image10]

The last thing to check is that we are excluding files from our build that we don’t want included in our webpage.  You might have stuff stored in your github.io page other than this template and we don’t want to accidentally build this in into your page:

![][image11]  
What other files do we want to look at?  Before modifying things extensifly, we can check a few more out.

**You can run an interactive version that will reload with your changes with “bundle exec jekyll serve \-l” but it will crash if you have another interactive instance going.  You can always do “bundle exec jekyll serve” and then manually refresh to see your changes.**

**\_plugins (directory)**

![][image12]

Some other interesting files to know about (but that you don’t need to edit) is the \_plugins – this is where the code to do interactive visualizations with vega-lite (like vegachart\_tags).  There are some other things listed here as well that we are really going to ignore. These plugins come from the [4dcu-be Jekyll template](https://github.com/4dcu-be/4dcu.be).

**assets**

Inside the assets folder there are a few folders that we will add things to.  In particular, we will store any screenshots/images in assets/pngs and any vega-lite output JSON’s in the json folder.  More on this when we get to making interactive plots on our webpage.  
![][image13]

**python\_notebooks**  
![][image14]  
This is where you can store “loose” python notebooks.  In theory, you will link to your analysis plots in whatever repositories are storing those analysis notebooks, but just in case you want to do something “quick and dirty” and link that notebook, you can put it here.  Check out the [README](https://github.com/jnaiman/online_cv_public/tree/main/python_notebooks) for updates, but that is the gist of this folder :) 

**\_layouts (directory)**  
![][image15]  
Another set of files that we won’t really mess with is the layouts in the \_layouts folder.  These are ways to define different layouts for different kinds of pages.  How our different pages look is also modified by things in the…

**\_includes (directory)**  
This also includes some info about how different pages will look.  
![][image16]  
For example, if we look in the \_includes/projects folder:  
![][image17]  
We see how each project card will look is probably determined in the project-card.html file and the general projects page is determined with the index.html

**\_example\_posts & \_example\_projects (directories)**  
![][image18]  
These two folders contain some example projects and blog posts you can look at.  Since we’ll be building our own in a bit, we won’t focus on these now, but they are there for you to come back to look at after we’ve started building our own to get some ideas.

**\_posts**  
![][image19]  
This contains a placeholder blog post if you want to talk about new things in your life, i.e. in a blog style.  Note the format of these with the filename starting with YYYY-MM-DD (year, month, date).

If you open this file up in a text editor, you’ll see that its mostly markdown:  
![][image20]  
With some yaml lines at the top that give specific parameters for each blog post, like title, any tags, color, etc.  See the \_example\_posts directory for more examples.  We won’t be focusing on blog posts for this class, but you can certainly check out the examples to get started if you want to blog.

**pages (directory)**  
![][image21]  
One small thing we might want to change in the pages directory – this is the projects.html file in which we can add github projects that are already \*under our github name\*.

![][image22]

In the example I’ve got the name of the repository that is associated with my main github page.  For reference, the URL of this repo is: 

https://github.com/jnaiman/is507\_spring2021

This shows up as an “automatic” card under our projects folder.  You won’t see \*my\* repository, even though it is included in the template you are using since it is not related to your repo\!

**pages/about.md**

Also in the pages directory is a file where you can modify some things for your “About” page.  In particular, you can modify your description a that appears at the top by editing the about.md file in a text editor:  
![][image23]  
In particular, you want to edit all the stuff above the \<div class…\> stuff (there are other files to edit for your skills section and your timeline\!\!).

**\_data**

This folder includes some files that are useful for your “About” page as well.  
![][image24]  
In particular:

**\_data/programming-skills.yml**

![][image25]

In this file, you can include your different *programming* skills along with your proficiency.  There are a few options to add something new:

* Name of language  
* Percentage of “skill” obtained – this is a bit fuzzy, but you can think of it as the % of the bar on the top that increases/decreases  
* The level – this is the text that will show up on the top  
* The color – what color you want to make this object  
  * Where do these colors come from? Check out the file: \_sass/\_variables.scss  
    

**\_data/other-skills.yml**  
![][image26]  
This file is very similar to the programming skills file, except it is a good place to list your various other skills.

**\_data/timeline.yml**  
![][image27]  
The final file you probably want to modify in this folder is your timeline.  For each entry you need:

* The title (is it a job, if so, what kind? Are you a student, if so what major?)  
* The start-end dates  
* A description (right now, the “standard” placeholder text)

Note this is **ORDER DEPENDENT**.  If we wanted our most recent position to be on top, we can re-order this to put that on top.  Whatever order it is in this file is the order it will show up on your About page timeline.

**\_projects (directory)**  
![][image28]  
Finally, we have your projects directory – this is where we will spend the majority of our time.  Here we will add projects that include interactive data visualizations.  The template is project 1, which is a vega-lite example.  

Note the formatting here – there is a 1\_ to indicate we want this project to come first in our list as it shows up on our projects page\!

If we open up this template file in a text editor:  
![][image29]  
We see a few things.  Like with the template blog post file, there are some yaml snippets at the top that change the name of the project, what tool tags you want to use, an image to show on the projects page and a description.

*Of vital importance\!  If you are using vega-lite to make interactive plots, you MUST include the custom\_js lines\!\!\!*

Other than those specifics, the rest of the file will be mostly written in markdown, with the occasional use of \<vegachart\> HTML tags that we will use to make interactive visualizations.

That is the end of our overview\!  Now we will dig a bit deeper into how to add projects and how to include vega-lite to make some interactive plots.  To do this, start with the vega-editor to make a quick example, then move to Python to start translating some of the stuff we’ve done on Starboard into this format.

Vega-lite-ho\!
